prompt:
EDIT the attached front left car reference as the base image.

COMPOSITION PRIORITY: an environment-led wide tracking shot, not a close-up vehicle beauty shot. The car must occupy only 52–58% of the full image width, with at least 12% breathing room at either bumper where the layout permits. Pull the camera back and extend the scene; never enlarge the car to fill unused space. Place the car below the upper 35% typography area, keeping both wheels above the bottom 12%. Surroundings should occupy most of the frame. Avoid a large empty blue-sky cap: allow 25–35% deep sky bounded by the diagonal infrastructure, with the reserved typography area kept clear. Keep the car visible and recognizable at this smaller scale. These framing requirements override the tight crop of the attached car cutout; use the reference only for car geometry, viewpoint and livery, not its size in the output.

This is an image-editing/background-replacement task, not a request to generate or redraw a new car from scratch. Use the original vehicle cutout wherever possible, compositing it into a photorealistic urban campaign photograph. Protect the car body and branding; replace or extend the surroundings, then integrate road contact shadows, lighting and panning effects around the original vehicle. If your tool supports masks, mask the surroundings for replacement while protecting the vehicle. Do not claim that a generative edit guarantees pixel-identical preservation; for exact branding, retain/composite the original car pixels rather than repainting the livery. Preserve the exact white sedan model, body proportions, wheels, grille, lights, windows, and WB Taxi livery from the reference, including the magenta/violet panel arrangement, door wordmark and number 260. Do not mirror, redesign or replace the car.

Windows and cabin: keep all windows fully closed. Use realistic dark reflective glazing, natural reflections of the surrounding architecture and sky, and a deeply shadowed cabin so no face is identifiable through the windshield or side windows. Preserve window transparency cues, glass edges and believable reflections; do not paint flat opaque black panels over the glass. If an occupant is visible at all, show only an indistinct silhouette behind the reflections, with no discernible eyes, mouth or facial features. Do not invent a visible driver portrait, open the window, brighten the cabin or expose a distorted face. Apply this to every angle, including front three-quarter views. Preserve the reference vehicle silhouette, mirrors and window geometry.

Omit the blank white front license plate and its mounting bracket: continue the grille pattern naturally behind it. Do not add any blank white number plates or placeholder rectangles at the front or rear.

Camera: low tracking camera near wheel height, with a slightly upward view revealing a long diagonal wall top against deep cobalt sky; keep the original vehicle viewpoint. Selected vehicle view: front-left three-quarter view, matching the reference viewpoint. Use the low, wide camera treatment described above. Show the entire vehicle, both bumpers and wheels, with breathing room around it.

Scene: a sunken expressway beside a single tall continuous white concrete retaining wall, its top edge forming one clean diagonal beneath open deep cobalt sky. One narrow recessed horizontal light strip and sparse structural seams give scale; the wall is infrastructure, not a windowless office facade. No windows, towers, storefronts or building skyline; keep the wall as broad low-detail tonal bands under panning blur. No trees, foliage, bushes or greenery anywhere, including reflections; no clouds. The selected street scene determines the architecture: do not replace walls, underpasses or open-road surroundings with a row of modern apartment buildings. If buildings are present, use just one or two broad, simple facade masses with large neutral surfaces. Suppress small windows, repetitive sharp facade grids, ornamental details, sharp distant skylines, street furniture and clusters of poles. Buildings are atmospheric color and light bands rather than an architectural subject. No crowds, prominent advertising, busy signage, traffic clutter or foreground obstructions.

Motion and light: the camera tracks the moving car at matching speed in a realistic panning shot. Keep the original car body and branding sharp and unchanged; show clearly visible rotational motion blur in the wheels and strong, long, coherent horizontal panning streaks across BOTH the building facades and road. Background windows, facade edges and road markings must visibly stretch into soft directional bands at normal viewing size. Gentle shallow depth of field or a slightly blurred road alone is not enough: the architecture must lose fine detail through motion. Aim for a slow-shutter tracking photograph, approximately 1/15–1/30 second, with the car tracked sharply. Keep the bodywork, WB Taxi wordmark, number 260 and every magenta/violet livery boundary tack sharp: no blur, smearing, warped letters, redrawn logos or altered graphic details on the car. Protect the original branded body pixels; apply motion blur only to separate background/road and wheel regions. If the tool cannot preserve the logo pixels exactly, retain the original car as a composited layer rather than regenerating its branding. bright clear summer daylight with neutral white balance, crisp natural highlights and defined tire contact shadows. Clean blue sky, no clouds, no sunset glow or orange color cast. Keep the white paint neutral and magenta/violet branding saturated and accurate. cool neutral silver-white concrete and deep navy road shadows. No honey-colored stone, amber glass, office windows or decorative facade piers. Daylight should be crisp blue and white; sunset adds only a restrained warm edge, never an overall golden filter Use neutral urban colors and rich violet/magenta brand accents. Follow the selected scene palette and structure; do not copy the warm office-building background or golden grading of another campaign image. Realistic tire contact and road shadow; no floating car, distorted geometry, radial zoom blur, speed-line graphics or blur across the branded bodywork.

Output aspect ratio 4:5. Compose the scene with a clean, low-detail typography-safe area in the upper 35% of the image. Extend the environment rather than filling the frame with the subject: use uncluttered sky, architecture, cabin surfaces or softly blurred road, with calm tonal contrast. Place the main subject outside this area; keep faces, hands, the complete car and its branding clear of future text. No generated text, placeholder lettering, graphic panels or artificial blank borders.  Leave the reserved area usable for a headline, supporting copy and partner block. Preserve subject proportions and leave breathing room for alternative crops. Keep the complete car inside the frame. No added captions, watermarks, UI, extra logos or graphic overlays.
